title: Triangles
statement: Each data line describes two sets of side lengths. Consider every one-to-one pairing of their sides. Find the largest number of equal side pairs. Each side can be used only once.
inputSpec: Five lines, each containing six positive decimal numbers. The first three describe the first triangle; the final three describe the second. Use spaces between input values. Do not include the paper worksheet’s numbered labels or commas.
outputSpec: One integer from 0 to 3 per input line.
constraints: Side lengths are positive decimals, at most 1000000.
Do not reject invalid triangles in the Junior or Intermediate version; only Senior requests validation.
hints: Try all vertex permutations; compare exact decimal values or cross-products.

title: Triangles
statement: Each data line describes two sets of side lengths. Consider every one-to-one pairing of their sides. The first triangle has vertices ABC and its sides are given in order AB, BC, AC. The second has vertices DEF and its sides are given in order DE, EF, DF. A name such as EFD means A corresponds to E, B to F, and C to D. Find a correspondence making all three paired side lengths equal.
inputSpec: Five lines, each containing six positive decimal numbers. The first three describe the first triangle; the final three describe the second. Use spaces between input values. Do not include the paper worksheet’s numbered labels or commas.
outputSpec: Print the corresponding three-letter name, or NONE if no correspondence makes all sides equal. If several names satisfy the rules, print the alphabetically first name. Print one answer per input line.
constraints: Side lengths are positive decimals, at most 1000000.
Do not reject invalid triangles in the Junior or Intermediate version; only Senior requests validation.
hints: Try all vertex permutations; compare exact decimal values or cross-products.

title: Triangles
statement: Each data line describes two sets of side lengths. Consider every one-to-one pairing of their sides. The first triangle has vertices ABC and its sides are given in order AB, BC, AC. The second has vertices DEF and its sides are given in order DE, EF, DF. A name such as EFD means A corresponds to E, B to F, and C to D. First check both sets with the strict triangle inequality: the sum of any two sides must exceed the third. Then find a correspondence for which all three ratios of corresponding side lengths are equal.
inputSpec: Five lines, each containing six positive decimal numbers. The first three describe the first triangle; the final three describe the second. Use spaces between input values. Do not include the paper worksheet’s numbered labels or commas.
outputSpec: Print NOT VALID if either set fails the triangle inequality; otherwise print the corresponding three-letter name, or NONE if no proportional correspondence exists. If several names satisfy the rules, print the alphabetically first name. Print one answer per input line.
constraints: Side lengths are positive decimals, at most 1000000.
Do not reject invalid triangles in the Junior or Intermediate version; only Senior requests validation.

samples.output:
DFE
DEF
EFD
NONE
NOT VALID

hints: Try all vertex permutations; compare exact decimal values or cross-products.

title: ACSL Bridge
statement: A bridge bid b promises b + 6 tricks. Clubs (C) and diamonds (D) score 20 points per contracted trick; hearts (H) and spades (S) score 30. No trump scores 40 for the first contracted trick and 30 for each remaining one. If the contract is made, these contracted points go below the line. Every extra trick scores above the line at 20 points for C/D and 30 for H/S/no trump.

outputSpec: For each line, print the below-line points and above-line points, separated by one space.
constraints: 1 ≤ bid ≤ 7; 0 ≤ tricks won ≤ 13.
hints: Track contracted points separately from overtricks and penalties.

title: ACSL Golf
statement: Golf scores are better when smaller. Report a cumulative score relative to the sum of the par values: use par for zero difference, x under par for a negative difference, and x over par for a positive difference. A hole is won only by a player whose score is strictly lower than every opponent’s score on that hole; ties do not win holes. The names of scores relative to one hole’s par are: -2 eagle, -1 birdie, 0 par, +1 bogey, +2 double bogey.
inputSpec: Four lines, each containing par and the player’s score. Use spaces between input values. Do not include the paper worksheet’s numbered labels or commas.
outputSpec: Print each hole’s score name on its own line, then a fifth line giving the four-hole total relative to par.
constraints: Par is 3, 4, or 5. Scores are positive and differ from par by at most 2.

birdie
double bogey
bogey
birdie
1 over par

hints: Keep per-hole comparisons separate from cumulative totals.

title: Draft Picks
statement: Each contract gives its length in years and total value in millions of dollars. The annual salary is total value divided by contract length. Guaranteed money, when supplied, is between 0 and the contract value.

title: ACSL Scrabble
statement: Score a four-letter word on a board with 4 rows and 10 columns, numbered 1–40 in row-major order. Horizontal placements move +1 per letter; vertical placements move +10. Letters score A/E=1, D/R=2, B/M=3, V/Y=4, J/X=8. Assign each square the first matching bonus in this priority order: numbers 3,9,15,… (square % 6 = 3) double the letter; otherwise multiples of 5 triple the letter; otherwise multiples of 7 double the word; otherwise multiples of 8 triple the word. All other squares have no bonus. Sum the modified letter values, then apply the word multipliers.
inputSpec: First line: four letters separated by spaces. Next five lines: one horizontal starting square. Use spaces between input values. Do not include the paper worksheet’s numbered labels or commas.
outputSpec: Print the word score for each placement.
constraints: Words use only A, E, D, R, B, M, V, Y, J, X.
Every placement fits entirely on the board without wrapping a row.
A tested placement contains at most one word-multiplier square.
hints: Apply the first matching square rule before any word multipliers.

title: ACSL CHMOD
statement: The three permission digits describe owner, group, others, in that order. Each octal digit 0–7 becomes exactly three binary bits, including leading zeroes. Bits 4,2,1 mean read, write, execute, represented by r,w,x; absent permissions are -. Keep a space between each group. Separate the two requested representations with the literal word and.
inputSpec: Five lines, each with three octal digits separated by spaces.
outputSpec: For each line print the binary groups, then and, then the permission groups; for example 101 010 110 and r-x -w- rw-.
constraints: Octal permission digits are 0–7.
Senior special digit is 0, 1, 2, or 4.
hints: Preserve leading zero bits when formatting each group.

title: ACSL CHMOD
statement: The three permission digits describe owner, group, others, in that order. Each octal digit 0–7 becomes exactly three binary bits, including leading zeroes. Bits 4,2,1 mean read, write, execute, represented by r,w,x; absent permissions are -. Keep a space between each group. Separate the two requested representations with the literal word and. A fourth digit comes BEFORE the three ordinary digits: 0=no special permission, 1=owner, 2=group, 4=others. Only if the affected class already has x, change that x to s for owner/group or t for others. This ACSL mapping is part of the problem; do not substitute a different operating-system convention.

constraints: Octal permission digits are 0–7.
Senior special digit is 0, 1, 2, or 4.
hints: Preserve leading zero bits when formatting each group.

title: ACSL Ninety-Nine
statement: Simulate the game until a card makes the running total exceed 99. The player who plays that card loses. Check for a loss immediately after applying a card; do not draw another card after the game ends. Unused supplied cards are ignored. Cards are 0–9. The player plays cards in arrival order (a queue). A 9 leaves the total unchanged; a 4 subtracts 10; a 0 adds 11 if that stays at most 99, otherwise adds 1. Other cards add their face value.
inputSpec: Five lines: initial total, three cards initially held by the player, then seven cards alternating player draw, dealer play, player draw, dealer play, and so on. The player moves first.
outputSpec: For each line print the final total and the winner: player or dealer, separated by a space.
constraints: Initial totals are 0–99.
Each supplied game is guaranteed to produce a winner before the necessary cards run out.
hints: Keep hand order separate from a card’s effect on the total.

title: ACSL Ninety-Nine

Play the highest FACE VALUE in the player’s hand, even when that card has a special effect. A 9 passes; T subtracts 10; A adds 14 if the result stays at most 99, otherwise adds 1. Other cards add their face value.

outputSpec: For each line print the final total and winner, player or dealer, separated by a space.
constraints: Initial totals are 0–99.

title: ACSL Ninety-Nine
statement: Simulate the game until a card makes the running total exceed 99. The player who plays that card loses. title: Digit Reassembly
statement: Answer five different questions about decimal integers: line 1 asks for the number of digits; line 2 for the digit sum; line 3 for the sum at odd 1-based positions from the LEFT; line 4 for the count of digit 4; line 5 for the middle digit. For an even length choose the left of the two middle digits.
inputSpec: Exactly five positive decimal integers, one per line.
outputSpec: Print the five answers, one per line.
constraints: Integers have 1–50 digits and no leading zero.
Intermediate: 1 ≤ n ≤ number of digits. Senior: 1 ≤ n ≤ 50; n may exceed the number’s length.
Use arithmetic that preserves all digits.
hints: Treat the input as a digit string so no digits are lost.

title: Digit Reassembly
statement: Read each integer as a decimal digit string; leading zeroes inside a selected group contribute normally. Starting at every position where n digits remain, take a consecutive length-n window. Windows overlap. Add the numeric values of all windows.
inputSpec: Five lines, each containing a positive decimal integer and a window length n.
outputSpec: Print the sum of the overlapping groups for each line.
constraints: Integers have 1–50 digits and no leading zero.
Intermediate: 1 ≤ n ≤ number of digits. Senior: 1 ≤ n ≤ 50; n may exceed the number’s length.
Use arithmetic that preserves all digits.
hints: Treat the input as a digit string so no digits are lost.

title: Digit Reassembly
statement: Read each integer as a decimal digit string; leading zeroes inside a selected group contribute normally. Split left to right into NON-overlapping groups of n digits. Pad the final short group with trailing zeroes to reach n digits, then add all group values.
inputSpec: Five lines, each containing a positive decimal integer and a group length n.
outputSpec: Print the sum of the padded groups for each line.
constraints: Integers have 1–50 digits and no leading zero.
Intermediate: 1 ≤ n ≤ number of digits. Senior: 1 ≤ n ≤ 50; n may exceed the number’s length.
Use arithmetic that preserves all digits.
hints: Treat the input as a digit string so no digits are lost.

title: Number Transformation
statement: Positions are counted from the RIGHT starting at 1. Let x be the original digit at position P. All changes are based on the original digits, not on digits already changed. If x is 0–4, replace it by the units digit of x+D. If x is 5–9, replace it by the LEFTMOST digit of |x−D| (the value 0 has digit 0). Replace every digit to its right by 0; leave digits to the left unchanged.
inputSpec: Five lines: positive integer N, position P, positive transition integer D.
outputSpec: One transformed digit string per line, without spaces.
constraints: 1 ≤ N < 10^15; P is a valid digit position.
Junior and Intermediate inputs do not produce a leading zero. Junior D is positive and at most 10^9.
hints: Use the original position digit for every replacement.

title: Number Transformation
statement: Positions are counted from the RIGHT starting at 1. Let x be the original digit at position P. All changes are based on the original digits, not on digits already changed. Replace every digit to the left of x with the units digit of its sum with x. Leave x unchanged. Replace every digit to its right with its absolute difference from x.
inputSpec: Five lines: positive integer N and position P.
outputSpec: One transformed digit string per line, without spaces.
constraints: 1 ≤ N < 10^15; P is a valid digit position.
Junior and Intermediate inputs do not produce a leading zero. Junior D is positive and at most 10^9.

title: Number Transformation
statement: Positions are counted from the RIGHT starting at 1. Let x be the original digit at position P. All changes are based on the original digits, not on digits already changed. Replace every digit to the left of x with its full sum with x, which can have two digits. Replace x with the number of DISTINCT prime factors of the original N. The number 1 has zero prime factors. Replace every digit to the right with its absolute difference from x. Concatenate the resulting pieces without separators.
inputSpec: Five lines: positive integer N and position P.
outputSpec: One transformed digit string per line, without spaces.
constraints: 1 ≤ N < 10^15; P is a valid digit position.
Junior and Intermediate inputs do not produce a leading zero. Junior D is positive and at most 10^9.
hints: Use the original position digit for every replacement.

title: Numeral Triangles
statement: Fill a triangle row by row: row 1 has one term, row 2 two, and row r has r. The untransformed sequence starts at s and increases by d for every position. title: ACSL Tiles
statement: Four rows begin with the four digits of originalRows, padding with leading zeroes when needed. A two-digit tile can be reversed. It matches a row when one end equals the row’s last digit; append the tile so the matching end touches the row. Start checking at row 1. After a placement, start the next search at the row AFTER the row just used, wrapping from row 4 to row 1. If the placed tile is a double, the next placement MUST be on that same row; this lock remains until a non-double is placed there. Process tiles once, in input order. For each tile, try rows in the prescribed cyclic order, or only the locked row. If it cannot be placed, discard it without changing the next-search position or lock. Add the two digits of every discarded tile.
inputSpec: Two lines: originalRows, then a space-separated list of tiles.
outputSpec: The sum of all individual digits on discarded tiles.
constraints: originalRows contains four digits 1–9.
The hand has 1–50 tiles; each tile has two digits from 1–9.
hints: Keep the next row and any double lock as explicit state.

title: ACSL Tiles
statement: Four rows begin with the four digits of originalRows, padding with leading zeroes when needed. A two-digit tile can be reversed. It matches a row when one end equals the row’s last digit; append the tile so the matching end touches the row. Start checking at row 1. After a placement, start the next search at the row AFTER the row just used, wrapping from row 4 to row 1. If the placed tile is a double, the next placement MUST be on that same row; this lock remains until a non-double is placed there. On each turn, scan the hand from its FIRST tile, trying each against rows in the prescribed order. Place the first tile that fits and restart scanning the remaining hand from the beginning. If no hand tile fits, draw tiles one at a time, appending them to the hand, until one can be placed. Stop as soon as the hand is empty, even if the draw pile is not; also stop when no hand tile fits and the draw pile is empty. Sum the individual digits remaining in the HAND, excluding undrawn tiles.
inputSpec: Three lines: originalRows, hand tiles separated by spaces, draw-pile tiles separated by spaces. An empty third line means no draw tiles. A token 0 is the tile 00, not an empty draw pile.
outputSpec: The sum of all individual digits on tiles left in the hand.
constraints: 0 ≤ originalRows ≤ 9999; use leading zero padding to obtain four row digits.
Each tile is 0–99; one-digit tiles are padded with a leading zero.
The hand has 1–50 tiles; the draw pile has 0–50 tiles.
hints: Keep the next row and any double lock as explicit state.
